summary: This note describes the geological origins of Arthur's Seat, a hill in Edinburgh. It was formed by an extinct Carboniferous volcanic system, with lava dated to 341 to 335 million years ago, and was later shaped by glacial erosion during the Quaternary. The note also explains how the Salisbury Crags formed and notes the hill's resemblance to a lion couchant.
one_line: Geological origins of Arthur's Seat, an Edinburgh hill formed by an extinct Carboniferous volcano and sculpted by Quaternary glaciation.
key_facts: Arthur's Seat was formed by an extinct volcano system of Carboniferous age, like the rock on which Edinburgh Castle is built.
Lava samples from Arthur's Seat have been dated at 341 to 335 million years old.
A glacier moving from west to east during the Quaternary eroded the volcanic system.
The Quaternary period covers approximately the last two million years.
Glacial erosion exposed rocky crags to the west and left a tail of material swept to the east.
The Salisbury Crags formed from this erosion and became basalt cliffs between Arthur's Seat and the city centre.
From some angles, Arthur's Seat resembles a lion couchant.
Two of the several extinct vents make up the 'Lion's Head' and the 'Lion's Haunch'.
